summary.text: Quadratic reciprocity makes \(5\) a square modulo \(p\); choosing the smaller of the two roots \(\pm r\) gives \(4\le r\le p/2\) and \(r^2-5=pm\). For \(n=r-1\), continuant identities and parity show that \(m\) divides the adjacent continuant while \(p\) does not, so reducing the continued fraction cancels exactly \(m\) and leaves denominator \(p\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
R_k(n)=k-\frac{k+1}{R_{k+1}(n)}\qquad(2\leq k<n-1),
\]
with
\[
R_{n-1}(n)=(n-1)-\frac n{-4}=(n-1)+\frac n4.
\]
Thus the continued fraction in the definition of the sequence is
\[
C_n=\frac1{R_2(n)}.
\]
The term \(a(n)\) is the denominator of \(C_n\) after reduction, equivalently the absolute value of the numerator of the reduced rational number \(R_2(n)\).

We shall prove that every prime \(p\equiv1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\) occurs in this way.

## 1. Integer continuants

It is convenient to put \(r=n+1\), so eventually we will take \(n=r-1\). For every \(r\geq4\), define integers
\[
X_{r-1}=4,\qquad X_{r-2}=5r-9,
\]
and, proceeding downward, define
\[
X_k=kX_{k+1}-(k+1)X_{k+2}
        \qquad(2\leq k\leq r-3).
\]
Here and below the dependence of the \(X_k\)'s on \(r\) is understood.

The base value of the continued fraction for \(n=r-1\) is
\[
R_{r-2}(r-1)=(r-2)+\frac{r-1}{4}
             =\frac{5r-9}{4}
             =\frac{X_{r-2}}{X_{r-1}}.
\]
Moreover, if
\(R_{k+1}(r-1)=X_{k+1}/X_{k+2}\), then
\[
R_k(r-1)
 =k-\frac{k+1}{X_{k+1}/X_{k+2}}
 =\frac{kX_{k+1}-(k+1)X_{k+2}}{X_{k+1}}
 =\frac{X_k}{X_{k+1}}.
\]
Consequently, provided \(X_3,X_4,\ldots,X_{r-1}\) are all nonzero, downward induction gives
\[
R_2(r-1)=\frac{X_2}{X_3}.                                      \tag{1}
\]
The nonvanishing condition will be proved for the particular \(r\) that we construct.

We need two identities for these continuants.

### First identity: \(X_2=r^2-5\)

For every \(k\) with \(2\leq k\leq r-2\), one has
\[
X_2=(k-1)X_k+\bigl(1-(k-1)^2\bigr)X_{k+1}.                    \tag{2}
\]
For \(k=2\), this just says \(X_2=X_2\). If (2) holds at \(k\), use
\(X_k=kX_{k+1}-(k+1)X_{k+2}\). The coefficient of \(X_{k+1}\) becomes
\[
k(k-1)+1-(k-1)^2=k,
\]
and the coefficient of \(X_{k+2}\) becomes
\[
-(k-1)(k+1)=1-k^2.
\]
This is precisely (2) with \(k+1\) in place of \(k\), proving the identity by induction.

Set \(k=r-2\) in (2) and use the two terminal values. We obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
X_2
 &= (r-3)(5r-9)+\bigl(1-(r-3)^2\bigr)4\\
 &=r^2-5.                                                       \tag{3}
\end{aligned}
\]

### Second identity: a forward invariant

Define integers \(W_k\) by
\[
W_2=1,\qquad W_3=0,
\]
and
\[
W_{k+2}=k(W_{k+1}-W_k)\qquad(k\geq2).
\]
Then for every \(2\leq k\leq r-1\),
\[
(k-1)!X_k=W_kX_2+2(k-2)X_3.                                  \tag{4}
\]
For \(k=2\), this is \(X_2=X_2\), and for \(k=3\), it is
\(2X_3=2X_3\). To perform the induction, rewrite the continuant recurrence as
\[
(k+1)X_{k+2}=kX_{k+1}-X_k.
\]
Multiplying by \(k!\) gives
\[
(k+1)!X_{k+2}
 =k\bigl(k!X_{k+1}-(k-1)!X_k\bigr).
\]
Substitution of (4) for \(k\) and \(k+1\) gives coefficient
\(k(W_{k+1}-W_k)=W_{k+2}\) on \(X_2\), and coefficient
\[
k\bigl(2(k-1)-2(k-2)\bigr)=2k
\]
on \(X_3\), exactly as required for the index \(k+2\). Thus (4) follows by induction.

## 2. Divisibility consequences of the forward invariant

We first record how a sufficiently small divisor of \(X_2\) must also divide \(X_3\).

Suppose that \(d>0\) is odd, \(d+1\leq r-1\), and \(d\mid X_2\). Apply (4) with \(k=d+1\):
\[
d!X_{d+1}=W_{d+1}X_2+2(d-1)X_3.
\]
The left side is divisible by \(d\), since \(d\mid d!\), and the first term on the right is divisible by \(d\), since \(d\mid X_2\). Hence
\[
d\mid 2(d-1)X_3.
\]
Because \(d\) is odd and \(\gcd(d,d-1)=1\),
\(\gcd(d,2(d-1))=1\). Therefore
\[
d\mid X_3.                                                    \tag{5}
\]

We also need a special statement for the factor \(4\). From the recurrence defining \(W_k\),
\[
W_4=-2,\qquad W_5=-6.
\]
Putting \(k=5\) in (4) gives
\[
24X_5=-6X_2+6X_3,
\]
or
\[
6X_3=24X_5+6X_2.                                               \tag{6}
\]
If \(4\mid X_2\), both terms on the right of (6) are divisible by \(8\). Thus \(8\mid6X_3\), so \(4\mid3X_3\). Since \(3\) and \(4\) are coprime,
\[
4\mid X_3.                                                     \tag{7}
\]
This argument applies when \(r\geq6\), so that \(X_5\) is among the continuants under consideration.

Combining (5) and (7), we have the following useful conclusion. Suppose \(m>0\),
\[
m+1\leq r-1,\qquad m\mid X_2,                                \tag{8}
\]
and either

* \(m\) is odd, or
* \(m=4u\) for an odd positive integer \(u\).

In the first case, (5) directly gives \(m\mid X_3\). In the second case, (8) implies \(r\geq6\), and it also implies that both \(4\) and \(u\) divide \(X_2\). By (7), \(4\mid X_3\), and by (5), \(u\mid X_3\). Since \(u\) is odd, \(\gcd(4,u)=1\), so \(4u=m\mid X_3\). Hence in either case
\[
m\mid X_3.                                                    \tag{9}
\]

We next establish two facts that will prevent unwanted cancellation and ensure that the continued fraction is defined at every stage. Let \(p\) be prime, let
\[
4\leq r\leq p-1,
\]
and suppose
\[
p\mid X_2.                                                    \tag{10}
\]
Then
\[
p\nmid X_3.                                                   \tag{11}
\]
Indeed, if \(p\mid X_3\) as well, put \(k=r-1\) in (4). Since \(X_{r-1}=4\), both terms on the right would be divisible by \(p\), and hence
\[
p\mid 4(r-2)!.
\]
But every positive factor occurring in \((r-2)!\) is less than \(p\), because \(r\leq p-1\), and in our eventual application \(p\geq11\), so \(p\nmid4\). This is impossible for a prime \(p\), proving (11).

More generally, for every \(j\) with \(3\leq j\leq r-1\),
\[
p\nmid X_j.                                                    \tag{12}
\]
For if \(p\mid X_j\), equation (4), together with \(p\mid X_2\), would imply
\[
p\mid 2(j-2)X_3.
\]
Here \(p\nmid2(j-2)\): the prime \(p\) is odd, and
\(0<j-2<p\). It would follow that \(p\mid X_3\), contradicting (11). In particular, none of \(X_3,\ldots,X_{r-1}\) is zero, because zero is divisible by \(p\). Thus equation (1) is applicable.

## 3. A small square root of \(5\) produces the term \(p\)

We now prove the central construction. Let \(p\) be an odd prime, and suppose there is an integer \(r\) satisfying
\[
4\leq r\leq \frac p2,
\qquad p\mid r^2-5.                                            \tag{13}
\]
Define the positive integer
\[
m=\frac{r^2-5}{p},
\]
so that
\[
r^2-5=pm.                                                      \tag{14}
\]
It is positive because \(r\geq4\).

We claim
\[
m\leq r-2.                                                     \tag{15}
\]
Indeed, \(r\leq p/2\) implies \(p\geq2r\). If instead \(m\geq r-1\), then (14) would give
\[
r^2-5=pm\geq2r(r-1).
\]
This is impossible for \(r\geq4\), since
\[
2r(r-1)-(r^2-5)=r^2-2r+5=(r-1)^2+4>0.
\]
Thus (15) holds, and equivalently \(m+1\leq r-1\).

The parity of \(m\) has exactly the form required above. There are two cases.

* If \(r\) is even, then \(r^2-5\) is odd. Since \(p\) is odd and \(pm=r^2-5\), \(m\) is odd.

* If \(r\) is odd, then \(r^2\equiv1\pmod8\), so
  \[
  r^2-5\equiv4\pmod8.
  \]
  Because \(p\) is odd, equation (14) implies that \(m\) is divisible by \(4\) but not by \(8\). Hence
  \[
  m=4u
  \]
  for an odd positive integer \(u\).

By (3) and (14),
\[
X_2=r^2-5=pm.                                                   \tag{16}
\]
Thus \(m\mid X_2\). The bound (15) and the parity alternatives just proved allow us to apply (9), obtaining \(m\mid X_3\). Write
\[
X_3=ms                                                       \tag{17}
\]
for some integer \(s\).

Since \(r\leq p/2<p\), the hypotheses used in (11) and (12) hold. Equation (16) gives \(p\mid X_2\), so (11) says \(p\nmid X_3\). From (17), this has two consequences:
\[
s\neq0\qquad\text{and}\qquad p\nmid s.                      \tag{18}
\]
Also, (12) shows that all \(X_3,\ldots,X_{r-1}\) are nonzero. We may therefore use (1), (16), and (17):
\[
R_2(r-1)=\frac{X_2}{X_3}
        =\frac{pm}{ms}
        =\frac p s.                                            \tag{19}
\]
Because \(p\) is prime and \(p\nmid s\), the integers \(p\) and \(s\) are coprime. Thus the reciprocal continued fraction is
\[
C_{r-1}=\frac{s}{p},
\]
and its reduced denominator is exactly \(p\). In other words,
\[
a(r-1)=p.                                                      \tag{20}
\]
We have proved: any root \(r\) of \(x^2\equiv5\pmod p\) lying in the interval \([4,p/2]\) produces an occurrence of \(p\) in the sequence.

## 4. Existence of the required small root

Let now \(p\) be prime and suppose
\[
p\equiv1\pmod {10}\quad\text{or}\quad p\equiv9\pmod {10}.
\]
In particular, \(p\neq2,5\), \(p\) is odd, and indeed \(p\geq11\).

Modulo \(5\), the two congruence classes give
\[
p\equiv1\pmod5\quad\text{or}\quad p\equiv4\pmod5.
\]
Both \(1\) and \(4\) are quadratic residues modulo \(5\). Hence the Legendre symbol \((p/5)\) equals \(1\). Since \(5\equiv1\pmod4\), quadratic reciprocity gives
\[
\left(\frac5p\right)=\left(\frac p5\right)=1.
\]
Therefore there is a nonzero residue \(z\pmod p\) such that
\[
z^2\equiv5\pmod p.                                           \tag{21}
\]
Choose its standard representative \(t\) with \(0\leq t<p\). It is nonzero, since otherwise (21) would imply \(p\mid5\), contrary to \(p\neq5\).

Of the two representatives \(t\) and \(p-t\) of the roots \(z\) and \(-z\), at least one is at most \(p/2\). Let \(r\) be that one. Then
\[
0<r\leq\frac p2,
\qquad r^2\equiv5\pmod p.                                     \tag{22}
\]
We also have \(r\geq4\). To see this, if \(r=0,1,2,3\), then
\[
r^2-5\in\{-5,-4,-1,4\}.
\]
Congruence (22) would say that \(p\) divides one of these nonzero integers. This is impossible because \(p\geq11\). Thus \(4\leq r\).

Since \(r\geq4\), the integer \(r^2-5\) is nonnegative, and (22) is exactly the divisibility
\[
p\mid r^2-5.
\]
All the hypotheses of the construction in Section 3 are now satisfied. Consequently, with
\[
n=r-1,
\]
equation (20) gives
\[
a(n)=p.
\]
Therefore every prime congruent to \(1\) or \(9\pmod {10}\) occurs in A363347, as claimed.
